The prime minister has promised fair pay for care workers, but new figures reveal the scale of what needs to change

Prime minister Andy Burnham visits Jewish Care in Golders Green. Image: Lauren Hurley / No 10 Downing Street

Care workers should be “the best paid people in society, not the worst”, according to prime minister Andy Burnham has said – but right now they barely earn more than the minimum wage.

When unveiling plans to overhaul adult social care in England this week, Burnham promised to create a National Care Service alongside the NHS.

“It can break people if they’re left without the support that they need,” he told an audience at a care home. “In fact, it does break people, and that needs to be recognised.”

Burnham has asked Baroness Louise Casey to report back next year with recommendations on how the new National Care Service should work. But one reform is already on the way, initiated by Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer: a fair pay agreement for care workers, setting minimum standards for pay and conditions across the sector, is due to come into force in April 2028.

Read more:

It is sorely needed. Frontline care workers earned, on average, just 79p above the minimum wage in 2024–25, according to new analysis by the Resolution Foundation. The median hourly wage was £12.60 – just 39p above the legal minimum.

“Social care staff perform a vital service,” said Hannah Slaughter, principal economist at the Resolution Foundation, “but that is not reflected in how they are valued by society.

“They are among the lowest-paid workers in Britain, are often subject to insecure contracts and constantly have to battle with staff shortages that make their jobs more intense.”

Around 21,000 care workers are being paid below the minimum wage illegally, the analysis suggests, though the true figure is likely to be higher. Home carers are often not paid for the time spent travelling between visits, meaning their ‘effective hourly wage’ can fall below the legal minimum.

A care worker with five or more years’ experience earns, on average, just 7p an hour more than someone starting the job, down from 33p in 2016.

One in five care workers is employed on a zero-hours contract, while more than a third of providers say better pay elsewhere is the main reason staff leave. Three in 10 say it is also the biggest obstacle to recruiting new workers.

Burnham acknowledged the reality facing many workers in his speech, pointing to “staff doing what they do on poverty pay.”

He added: “I’ve been made aware of somebody homeless working in a care setting, living out of a mobile home.”

The fair pay agreement, Slaughter said, “should help to address many of these issues, especially if complemented by better progression routes both within care and into the NHS”.

She added: “This should encourage more people to consider care as a career.”

A better staffed and more affordable social care system for families should ease the pressure on unpaid carers.

There are 4.7 million unpaid carers in England, according to Carers UK, and around 600 people give up paid work every day to care for a loved one. More than half say they are providing more care than they were a year ago, while eight in 10 have experienced problems with social care services.

More than a third of carers who left employment said more affordable, accessible or reliable social care services would have stopped them from having to quit.

Emily Holzhausen, director of policy and public affairs at Carers UK, welcomed Burnham’s announcement but warned the scale of the challenge should not be underestimated.

“In the sixteen years since the last white paper set out the fundamentals of a National Care Service, the scale and complexity of the problems with social care have grown far worse,” she said. “There are chronic shortages of care, high costs and challenging systems placing families providing unpaid care under extreme pressure.”

“We want unpaid carers’ futures to be at the heart of this conversation. It’s conversation that affects us all. Almost all of us will either provide unpaid care or receive care at some point in our lives.”
